newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yen's fall below 120 may spur Japan inflation fear.
newsitem.headline: Yen's fall below 120 may spur Japan inflation fear.

text.p: Japan may be faced with a fresh threat of inflation -- or worst yet, "stagflation" the a combination of economic stagnation and inflation -- as the tumbling yen pushes up import costs, analysts said on Thursday.
"There are worries over domestic prices. A long period of deflation has been coming to an end," said Akiyoshi Takumori, chief economist at Sakura Securities Co Ltd.

The "double trouble" of a 50 percent fall in the yen since the spring of 1995 and rising global commodity prices is seen filtering through the distribution system to push domestic prices up, analysts said.
This would also put pressure on interest rates and make it difficult for monetary authorities to manage credit policy amidst a fragile stock market and a lack of a strong recovery in the economy.
Japan, despite its heavy reliance on most raw materials for imports, has enjoyed low inflation. Higher raw material prices have been offset by internal cost-cutting efforts.
But such measures will hit their limit if the yen keeps falling, industry officials said.
"If the yen moves beyond 120 yen (against the dollar), fears of cost-boosting inflation may emerge," said Yoshihiro Yasunaga, managing director at Cosmo Oil Co Ltd.
Overall wholesales prices for December rose 0.9 percent from a year again while consumer prices were up 0.5 percent in November.
But there were more worrying signs. In 1996 trade figures released on Thursday, the government said that crude oil imports were 48 percent more expensive than the year before.
The yen dropped to a fresh 47-month low of 119.45 yen to the dollar on Thursday, nearly a 50 percent retracement from its record high of 79.75 yen to the dollar in April 1995.

Susumu Takahashi, a senior economist at Japan Research Institute Ltd said: "Around the 125 yen level would be the key point.. The more the yen weakens beyond that point, the more visible the adverse impact on the economy will be."
There has been a positive effect of a weaker yen as consumer prices are relatively stable at home even as import prices rise, while exporter profits are boosted, he added.

Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference on Wednesday that a weaker yen was not yet affecting overall domestic prices. But a central bank source said :"We must watch out for the possibility of inflation, driven by (rising) import costs and led by a weaker yen."

Government officials loudly warned against an excessive fall in the yen in the past weeks but currency dealers have defied such words as mere words with no action in sight, and continued their attempt to push the dollar above 120 yen.
Market operators are betting that Japan cannot openly sell dollars to halt the yen's falls since the United States and European nations are satisfied with the recent strength of the dollar.
Japan's economic recovery is also seen stalled.
Economists said that the chances were slim for now that the BOJ will raise its interest rates to halt the fall in the yen and check inflation pressures.

But they warn that a continued fall in the yen and the resulting upward pressure on interest rates would make it hard for the central bank to maintain its rock-bottom interest rates, which now stands at a record low of 0.5 percent.

The BOJ and the government have insisted that the economy has gradually recovered, but analysts said its strength is still uncertain after April, when the government will raise sales tax and end a special tax break.
